text: Design a stock spanner. Each call to next, with today's price, returns the span: the number of consecutive days, up to and including today, whose price was less than or equal to today's price.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — prices arrive one at a time, online, the span counts backward and includes today, and equal prices count, since it's less than or equal. Right?
Correct. There can be up to ten to the fourth calls.
So the span really ends at the previous strictly greater price. Everything from there up to today is less than or equal to today, and one strong day can absorb several weaker ones.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to store every price and walk backward on each call. That's linear per call, quadratic overall. This problem reminds me of a monotonic stack, and it fits because once a higher price arrives, the cheaper days before it can never stop a later span on their own. I keep a stack of price and span pairs, with prices decreasing. When today's price is greater than or equal to the top price, I absorb that block's span instead of recounting its days. That makes each call amortized constant time.

Here's the plan. One: start the span at one, for today. Two: while the top price is less than or equal to today's, add the top's span and pop. Three: push today's price with its span, and return the span. One thing worth flagging — I store the span with each price, not just the price. The popped block's span already encodes how many days it represents, so I add it in one step rather than recounting. I use less-than-or-equal so equal prices are absorbed, and I read the top's span before popping. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. The class holds one stack of price and span pairs. In next, span starts at one; a while loop folds in every block whose price is less than or equal to today's, then I push today's pair and return the top's span, which is exactly the span I just pushed. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — I must read the top's span before popping, or I'd lose the count I'm folding in.

Let's dry-run one hundred, eighty, sixty, seventy, sixty, seventy-five, eighty-five. Expected spans: one, one, one, two, one, four, six. The row that matters is the last call, eighty-five. It folds in seventy-five with span four and eighty with span one, plus today — four plus one plus one is six. Note that the seventy-five block had already compressed the sixty and seventy before it, so the accumulation is layered — that's why it stays amortized constant time. That matches. Let's also test corner cases. A strictly decreasing stream: every span is one and the stack keeps growing. All-equal prices like five, five, five: spans one, two, three, since less-than-or-equal absorbs equals.

The time complexity is amortized constant per call. Each price is pushed once and popped at most once, so across n calls the total work is linear. The space complexity is linear, for the stack. Oh, one more thing — this is the previous-greater pattern. It's the same monotonic stack idea as finding the next greater value, just looking into the past instead of the future, which is why it works online.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You stored the span with each price, so you accumulate instead of recounting. You used less-than-or-equal deliberately, to include equal prices. And you gave a crisp amortized argument, and connected it to the broader previous-greater pattern. Good work.
